doc.title: Luis Conte interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 24, 2025

title: Modern production: wallpaper music, copy and paste and lined-up horns
summary: Responding to Lou Marini's quote, Conte criticizes formulaic pop, home recording, and sessions where parts are copy-pasted and horns are quantized, as in a Thriller horn story.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Yeah. They send you a track and you can add. Yeah. I have another quote here. I’m sure the studio scene, as you mentioned, has changed a lot. And this is from your James Taylor bandmate, Lou Marini. And he was talking about the way songs are put together these days, and he said, “When I listen to these vocoder vocals and the rhythm tracks you could just as easily be listening to a washing machine. Luis Conte is a master percussionist. He’s always playing stuff for us from African tribal music, Caribbean, Brazilian. It’s so much more complex. The grooves are so intense that it makes the electronic stuff seem stupid. It seems infantile compared to what humans do naturally.”

Totally agreed. Of course. Man, you know what I call – and I work on some of these, I could tell you some things that man, what are some of these, you know the modern music that you hear on the radio. It sounds like wallpaper music to me. That’s what I call it. I call it wallpaper music. It’s just wallpaper. It’s almost – you know do you notice the wallpaper? No? So, it doesn’t matter. There’s like a formula. And it’s not only sad man, you have this one artist becomes a huge hit, now you have every record company has their artist that is like that artist. What happened to diversity? That’s what’s going on now man. So you go back to the tribal stuff man. That’s why I play these guys all kinds of stuff. They love it. And Gadd and those guys. Yeah. It’s another world now. And the machines, you know what about this? I will go in and work on a song. If I’m doing it in my house that doesn’t happen. I play the first chorus, I play the second chorus, and I play the outro. But nowadays I’ve done sessions, big acts man, big artists. And you play the
first chorus, I play, let’s say I play congas, I play whatever, three, four, five instruments. “Okay we got it.”
I was afraid you were going to say that. They’re just copy and pasting, right?

Copy/paste. I said, “What do you mean you got it, man?” “Yeah, yeah, well” – I remember doing this one – I’m not mentioning who they were but they wanted something timbale fills. And I did the timbale fills on the first chorus. They says, “Okay we’re good.” I said, “Bro, you’re not good, I mean you’re going to play the same fills” I mean whatever. You know. You know you don’t have to argue with them. I’ll tell you another – you want to know a story that’s kind of crazy? I go in to do a session. And I had already – I knew who the horn players that were before me, there was a session before me with a section. It was Dan Higgins and Jerry Hay and the late Gary Grant and Bill Reichenbach. You know, those four guys that played on all the Michael Jackson, all the great stuff. And I know they had been there because I had been working with them earlier and they said no we’re going over there to work. So I said okay, I’m going to be there at 7. So I get there for my 7 o’clock session and I’m recording. And then they go, “Let’s take a break.” And in another room I hear horns. And it’s those guys are the horns that just – and I walk in and I go, “Hey, how you guys doing?” “All right.” “What are you guys doing?” He says, “Oh man, yeah, we just have the horn section – we’re lining up the horns.” I said, “You’re lining up the horns?” You know Michael Jackson’s “Thriller?” Those are the guys on that record. They didn’t line those horns up back then. You know horn players breathe a certain way. The reason why they call those four guys to do all these record dates that are so funky on Al Jarreau or Michael Jackson. Whatever, you name it. The reason why they call them is because it’s a section. And they breathe a certain way and they play together and it’s just the beauty of the thing. “You guys are lining this shit up? What?”

I know what you mean. Because they can see the waveforms, they can literally like move something incrementally. Oh good Lord. in other words let’s take all the human feel out of this. It’ll be better.
There you go. That’s what’s up. That’s 2025.
